moves.spoken: The knight develops to f3, Black answers with the knight to c6, and we pin with the bishop to b5 — the Ruy Lopez, our main weapon.
Black plays the knight to f6 — the Berlin.
There are many ways to face the Berlin, but we go straight in — heading for the Berlin endgame, to show it's more than a draw.
Black declines the Berlin endgame with ...d6 — passive, but a legitimate Steinitz Defence.
Previously we'd prepare with c3; now, at a higher level, we play the more topical immediate d4.
Black takes on d4. We open the centre precisely because Black has played passively.
Black develops the bishop to d7.
We develop the knight to c3, opening things up to press our lead in development.
Black plays the bishop to e7.
Theory says take on c6 with the bishop, keeping our knight strongly centralized.

Black recaptures with the b-pawn, taking a defect into his queenside structure. Now the point: Black wants ...c5 to kick our knight, and we'd love to answer with the knight to f5 — but playing it right now lets Black trade it, and recapturing with a pawn would wreck our kingside and pull a pawn from the centre; b4 would be artificial. We don't need to prevent ...c5 at all — we prepare our response to it. Prophylaxis cuts both ways: you can stop a move, or ready an answer to it. The queen to f3 is best — it improves a piece and readies the knight to f5 the moment ...c5 arrives.
